theory.intro: A **unit vector** has magnitude exactly $1$, so it fixes a direction without a size. The **zero vector** $\underset{\sim}{0}$ has magnitude $0$ and no direction at all.
facts: $\underset{\sim}{i}$ is the unit vector one unit to the right, and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ is the unit vector one unit up.
A vector is a unit vector only when its magnitude is exactly $1$, so a short vector is not automatically a unit vector.
There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction.
$\underset{\sim}{0}$ is a vector, not the number $0$, so it can never equal a scalar.
The zero vector is drawn as a single point, and that point does not mark a position.
steps: Find the magnitude of the vector
Call it a unit vector when the magnitude is exactly $1$
Call it the zero vector when the magnitude is $0$, and give it no direction

foundation.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ is the standard horizontal unit vector.
It is a move of $1$ unit to the right.

$\underset{\sim}{j}$ is the standard vertical unit vector.
It is a move of $1$ unit upwards.

Both $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ are unit vectors, so each has magnitude $1$.
$|\underset{\sim}{i}|=1$ and $|\underset{\sim}{j}|=1$

foundation.question_text:
Is $-\underset{\sim}{j}$ a unit vector?
Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
$-\underset{\sim}{j}$ has the same length as $\underset{\sim}{j}$ and points the opposite way, so it is a move of $1$ unit downwards.
Its magnitude is $1$, so it is a unit vector; the direction a unit vector points in does not matter.

foundation.question_text:
An arrow representing $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is drawn only $0.4$ cm long on a diagram where $1$ cm represents $1$ unit.
A student says $\underset{\sim}{a}$ must be a unit vector because it is short.
Explain the error.
foundation.solution_text:
A unit vector must have magnitude exactly $1$, not merely a small magnitude.
Here the magnitude is $0.4$, so $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is not a unit vector.

Both terms are the same vector, $5\underset{\sim}{b}$, so subtracting removes all of its length.
$5\underset{\sim}{b}-5\underset{\sim}{b}=\underset{\sim}{0}$

Multiplying by the scalar $0$ shrinks the arrow until it has no length left.
$0\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{0}$

foundation.question_text: State the magnitude of $\underset{\sim}{0}$, and explain why no direction can be given for it.
foundation.solution_text:
$|\underset{\sim}{0}|=0$
An arrow of zero length is just a point, and a point has no arrowhead, so there is no direction to read.

$\underset{\sim}{p}$ spans $1$ square, so $|\underset{\sim}{p}|=1$.
$\underset{\sim}{q}$ spans $2$ squares, so $|\underset{\sim}{q}|=2$.
$\underset{\sim}{r}$ spans $1$ square, so $|\underset{\sim}{r}|=1$.
$\underset{\sim}{p}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}$ are the unit vectors.

foundation.question_text: Explain why $\underset{\sim}{0}$ is not the same thing as the number $0$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{0}$ is a vector, and the number $0$ is a scalar.
A vector and a scalar are different kinds of quantity, so they can never be equal, even though the magnitude of $\underset{\sim}{0}$ is the number $0$.

development.question_text: Describe $4\underset{\sim}{i}$ as a movement on a grid, and write down its magnitude.
development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ is $1$ unit to the right, and the scalar $4$ makes the arrow four times as long in the same direction.
$4\underset{\sim}{i}$ is a move of $4$ units to the right, and $|4\underset{\sim}{i}|=4$.

development.question_text: Describe $-3\underset{\sim}{j}$ as a movement on a grid, and write down its magnitude.
development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{j}$ is $1$ unit up, and the scalar $-3$ makes the arrow three times as long in the opposite direction.
$-3\underset{\sim}{j}$ is a move of $3$ units down, and $|-3\underset{\sim}{j}|=3$.

development.question_text:
Is $2\underset{\sim}{i}$ a unit vector?
Give a reason.
development.solution_text:
$2\underset{\sim}{i}$ is twice as long as $\underset{\sim}{i}$, so its magnitude is $2$.
A unit vector must have magnitude exactly $1$, so $2\underset{\sim}{i}$ is not a unit vector.

development.question_text:
$\underset{\sim}{d}$ points north-west and $|\underset{\sim}{d}|=1$.
Is $\underset{\sim}{d}$ a unit vector?
Give a reason.
development.solution_text:
The test for a unit vector is the magnitude alone.
$|\underset{\sim}{d}|=1$, so $\underset{\sim}{d}$ is a unit vector, even though it does not point along $\underset{\sim}{i}$ or $\underset{\sim}{j}$.

development.question_text:
A courier rides $3$ km due east from the depot, then rides the same $3$ km back to the depot.
Write down the displacement vector for the whole trip, and give a reason.
development.solution_text:
The ride out is $3$ km east and the ride back is $3$ km west, which is its negative.
The two legs have equal magnitude and opposite direction, and the courier finishes at the depot.
The displacement for the whole trip is $\underset{\sim}{0}$.

development.question_text: Explain why the zero vector is drawn as a single point, and why that point does not show a position.
development.solution_text:
The zero vector has magnitude $0$, so the tail and the head of the arrow are in the same place and the arrow shrinks to a point.
A vector carries only a magnitude and a direction, never a location, so the point can be drawn anywhere and still be the same zero vector.

development.question_text:
How many different unit vectors are there in two dimensions?
Explain your answer.
development.solution_text:
A unit vector is fixed by its direction, because its magnitude is always $1$.
There is one unit vector for every direction, and there are infinitely many directions, so there are infinitely many unit vectors.

development.question_text:
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ both have magnitude $1$.
State one further property that the pair $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ has.
development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ points along the $x$-axis and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ points along the $y$-axis.
The axes meet at a right angle, so $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ are perpendicular.

The only vector with magnitude $0$ is the zero vector.
$\underset{\sim}{v}=\underset{\sim}{0}$, so it has no direction.

mastery.question_text:
$\underset{\sim}{a}$ has magnitude $1$ and points due south, $\underset{\sim}{b}=-\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}$.
State whether each of $\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\underset{\sim}{c}$ is a unit vector, the zero vector, or neither, giving a reason for each.
mastery.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{b}$ has the same magnitude as $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and points due north.
$|\underset{\sim}{b}|=1$, so $\underset{\sim}{b}$ is a unit vector.
$\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{a}+(-\underset{\sim}{a})$
$=\underset{\sim}{0}$, so $\underset{\sim}{c}$ is the zero vector.

mastery.question_text: For each of $5\underset{\sim}{i}$, $-\underset{\sim}{i}$, $\underset{\sim}{0}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$, write down its magnitude and state whether it is a unit vector.
mastery.solution_text:
$|5\underset{\sim}{i}|=5$, so it is not a unit vector.
$|-\underset{\sim}{i}|=1$, so it is a unit vector pointing $1$ unit to the left.
$|\underset{\sim}{0}|=0$, so it is not a unit vector; it is the zero vector.
$|\underset{\sim}{j}|=1$, so it is a unit vector.

mastery.question_text:
A student writes two statements: '$\underset{\sim}{0}$ is a unit vector, because it has no length to worry about' and '$\underset{\sim}{i}$ is just the number $1$'.
Correct both statements.
mastery.solution_text:
A unit vector has magnitude exactly $1$, while $|\underset{\sim}{0}|=0$, so $\underset{\sim}{0}$ is the zero vector and not a unit vector.
$\underset{\sim}{i}$ is a vector of magnitude $1$ pointing to the right, while $1$ is a scalar with no direction, so the two are different kinds of quantity.
